title: The Tannisho, part one
hook: read Shinran's sayings as remembered by his student
tomorrow: the student who wrote it all down was worried. about what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole moon and the whole sky in one dewdrop, and a fish that never leaves the water. The moon in a dewdrop. Today, a teacher's words, written down by someone who loved him.
screen: `THE MOON IN A DEWDROP.` → `A TEACHER'S WORDS, REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Some creators call their followers a family; some coaches post about their students like trophies. Shinran, the Japanese Pure Land teacher, had people walking long roads to hear him. And in the Tannisho, the short record of his sayings kept by his student Yuien, Shinran says, in paraphrase: I don't have even one disciple. Not one. Coming from a teacher with followers, that sounds like false modesty. It isn't.
screen: `FOLLOWERS AS TROPHIES.` → `SHINRAN: NOT ONE DISCIPLE.` → `NOT FALSE MODESTY.`

segments.voice: Here's his reason, in paraphrase. If I brought people to say the nembutsu, the name of Amida Buddha, by my own effort, they'd be my disciples. But they say it because Amida's working moves them. So how could I call them mine? That's other power, tariki: the trust and the practice come from Amida's vow, not from the teacher's skill or the student's. The same record opens on this note. When the thought of saying the nembutsu arises, Yuien remembers Shinran saying, a person is already embraced, never to be abandoned, and the vow doesn't sort people by young or old, good or bad. Then, a line that widens the circle: Shinran says he never once said the nembutsu for his own parents alone, because every living being has been his father and mother, brother and sister, through countless lives. Everyone is family. A neighbor tradition knows the shape of this. In the King James Version, Paul writes: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.” Shared: something given, not earned, and no room to boast. And an honest difference. For Paul, grace is the gift of God, the creator, through Christ. For Shinran, the gift is the vow of Amida, a Buddha, and Shin Buddhists don't speak of Amida as the maker of the world. Close cousins, and not the same. Other power, either way, is the end of keeping score.
screen: `NOT ONE DISCIPLE.` · `TARIKI: THE VOW DOES THE WORK.` · `EVERY BEING HAS BEEN FAMILY.` · `PAUL: GRACE, THE GIFT OF GOD.` · then, large: `OTHER POWER.`

segments.voice: Count, slowly, things in your life you didn't earn: the language you speak, someone who taught you to read, a meal someone else cooked, the breath arriving right now. One finger for each. When the count runs out, keep breathing, and notice that the breath isn't something you're making happen, until the bell.
The Tannisho: a short record of Shinran's sayings, written down by his student Yuien. In its first part, the teacher won't call anyone his own.
Your line: other power, a gift with no score kept. Part one of Shinran's sayings, read.

howItsDone: In Jodo Shinshu (Shin Buddhism), members say the nembutsu, Namu Amida Butsu, as an expression of gratitude rather than a technique, and the Tannisho is widely read in study groups.

notes: Tannisho chapters 1, 5 and 6 paraphrased (no public-domain English translation on the validator's list). Confirm: chapter 6's reasoning (if by my own effort, they'd be my disciples; but they say the nembutsu by Amida's working); chapter 1's 'embraced, never to be abandoned' and no distinction of young and old, good and evil; chapter 5's 'never once for my parents' sake alone' (the text says he never said it for the repose of his parents, since all beings have been parents and siblings). The script adds 'alone' for clarity; confirm or cut.

Unity thread (wisdom day, owner request: one human race, more alike than we think): Shinran's 'every being has been family' and the neighbor tradition's grace (Ephesians 2:8, KJV). Shared: a gift not earned, no boasting. Honest difference: for Paul, grace is God's gift through Christ; for Shinran, Amida Buddha's vow, and Shin Buddhists don't call Amida creator. A Christian reader and a Shin Buddhist reader should check the one-line descriptions. Christians differ among themselves on how grace and works fit; the script doesn't enter that.
